subject: Cloud Computing
title: Defense in Depth
description: A quick, practical guide to Defense in Depth.

hook.text: A castle has walls, a moat, guards, and locked doors. Cloud security uses the same layered approach.

buildup.text: Defense in depth means multiple security layers: network, identity, application, data, and monitoring.

discovery.text: If one layer fails, the next catches the threat. No single control is expected to stop everything.

twist.text: Many teams focus only on the perimeter. Once an attacker gets inside, there's nothing else stopping them.

climax.text: Defense in depth assumes every layer will eventually be breached. The goal is to slow and detect, not just prevent.

punchline.text: One lock can be picked. Five layers take much longer to break.

quiz.question: What is the core principle of defense in depth?
options: Multiple overlapping security layers so no single failure is catastrophic
One extremely strong firewall that blocks all threats
Keeping all data offline and disconnected from the internet

details.summary: Defense in depth layers multiple security controls so that if one fails, others still protect the environment. In cloud architectures, this means combining IAM, network controls, encryption, logging, and application security rather than relying on any single defense.
details.whyItMatters: No single security control is foolproof. Layered defenses ensure that attackers must bypass multiple independent barriers, dramatically reducing the probability of a successful breach.
takeaways: Combine identity, network, data, and application protections
No single control should be a single point of failure

faq.question: What are the typical layers in cloud defense in depth?
faq.answer: Physical security of data centers, network controls like firewalls and segmentation, identity and access management, application security including WAFs, data encryption at rest and in transit, and monitoring with logging and alerting form the standard layers.

faq.question: How does defense in depth apply to a serverless architecture?
faq.answer: Even without servers to manage, you still need IAM policies, function-level permissions, API authentication, input validation, secrets management, encrypted environment variables, and comprehensive logging. The layers shift but the principle remains identical.
